lessonTitle: Orbital Motion: Circular, Escape and Elliptical Orbits

blocks.text: The International Space Station circles Earth every 92 minutes at about 7.7 km/s, and it never needs an engine to keep up that speed. It is not 'above gravity'; it is falling freely, fast enough that the ground curves away beneath it as quickly as it drops. The same two conservation laws, energy and angular momentum, give its speed, its period, the speed needed to leave Earth altogether, and the changing speed of any elliptical orbit.

blocks.markdown: A satellite of mass $m$ moves under the gravitational attraction of a much heavier central body of mass $M$. Newton's law gives an inverse-square force of magnitude $GMm/r^2$ directed toward the centre. It is convenient to combine $G$ and $M$ into the **gravitational parameter** $\mu=GM$ (m$^3$/s$^2$). For Earth, a representative value is $\mu=3.986\times10^{14}$ m$^3$/s$^2$ and the mean radius is $R_E=6.371\times10^6$ m. We assume a point or spherical central mass, no drag and no other bodies.

blocks.title: Gravitational potential energy
blocks.text: For the inverse-square force the potential energy per unit mass at distance $r$ is $-\mu/r$ (zero at infinity, negative when bound). The specific mechanical energy $\varepsilon=\tfrac12v^2-\mu/r$ (J/kg) is constant along the orbit, and the specific angular momentum $h=rv_\theta$ (m$^2$/s) is also constant.

blocks.caption: Both hold for any motion under the inverse-square attraction of a fixed central body.

blocks.markdown: **Circular orbit.** For a circular path of radius $r$, gravity provides the centripetal force: $m v^2/r=m\mu/r^2$, so the speed is independent of the satellite's mass. The period follows from distance over speed. Higher circular orbits are slower and have longer periods, with $T\propto r^{3/2}$ (Kepler's third law).

blocks.title: Low Earth orbit
blocks.prompt: A satellite is in a circular orbit 400 km above Earth's surface. Find its speed and period (use $\mu=3.986\times10^{14}$ m$^3$/s$^2$ and $R_E=6371$ km).

steps.text: Orbit radius is measured from Earth's centre.

blocks.markdown: **Escape velocity.** A body leaves the central body's pull if its total energy is zero or positive, so that it can reach $r\to\infty$ with $v\ge0$. Setting $\varepsilon=0$ at launch from radius $R$ (ignoring atmosphere and rotation) gives the escape speed. Note it is $\sqrt2$ times the circular-orbit speed at the same radius.

blocks.title: Escape from Earth's surface
blocks.prompt: Find the escape speed from Earth's surface ($\mu=3.986\times10^{14}$ m$^3$/s$^2$, $R_E=6.371\times10^6$ m).

steps.text: Set the total energy to zero.
Compare with circular speed at the surface.

blocks.answer: The escape speed is about 11.2 km/s (independent of the body's mass).

blocks.markdown: **Elliptical orbits.** In an ellipse the distance varies between the closest point, **perigee** (radius $r_p$), and the farthest, **apogee** (radius $r_a$). At both points the velocity is perpendicular to the radius, so $h=r_pv_p=r_av_a$. Combining this with energy conservation determines both speeds from the two radii. The satellite moves fastest at perigee and slowest at apogee.

blocks.title: Speeds at perigee and apogee
blocks.prompt: A satellite orbits Earth with perigee radius $7.0\times10^6$ m and apogee radius $21.0\times10^6$ m. Find the speeds at perigee and apogee.

steps.text: Angular momentum gives the apogee speed.
Check: specific energy at each point is the same.

blocks.caption: Classification of orbits by speed at a given radius. Remember that $r$ is measured from the centre of the planet, not its surface.

points: Circular orbit: $v_c=\sqrt{\mu/r}$ and $T=2\pi\sqrt{r^3/\mu}$, both independent of the satellite's mass.
Escape speed from radius $R$ is $\sqrt{2\mu/R}=\sqrt2\,v_c$, obtained by setting the total energy to zero.
In an elliptical orbit $r_pv_p=r_av_a$ and energy is conserved, so the satellite is fastest at perigee and slowest at apogee.

questions.stem: Two satellites orbit Earth in circles of radius $r$, one of mass 100 kg and the other of mass 1000 kg. Their orbital speeds are

options.text: The 1000 kg satellite is ten times faster

questions.explanation: Gravity supplies the centripetal force, $mv^2/r=m\mu/r^2$, and the satellite's mass cancels. The circular speed depends only on $\mu$ and $r$.

questions.stem: A satellite's circular orbit radius is increased by a factor of four. Its period increases by a factor of
questions.explanation: From $T=2\pi\sqrt{r^3/\mu}$, the period scales as $r^{3/2}$, so quadrupling $r$ multiplies $T$ by $4^{3/2}=8$. Higher orbits are therefore much slower to circle the planet.

questions.stem: For a body leaving a planet's surface, the escape speed compared with the circular orbit speed at the surface is

distractorRationale.c: Escape needs more energy than circular orbit.
distractorRationale.d: Escape cannot be easier than orbit.

questions.explanation: The escape speed is $\sqrt{2\mu/R}$ and the circular speed is $\sqrt{\mu/R}$, so their ratio is $\sqrt2\approx1.41$. This is why escaping needs a speed that is about 41% more than circling at the same radius.

questions.stem: A satellite moves in an elliptical orbit about Earth. At which point is its speed greatest?

options.text: At the ends of the minor axis

distractorRationale.d: Constant speed occurs only in a circular orbit.

questions.explanation: Angular momentum conservation gives $r_pv_p=r_av_a$, so the smallest radius corresponds to the largest speed. The satellite also has the lowest potential energy there.

questions.stem: A spacecraft at radius $r$ from Earth's centre has a speed $v$ in the direction perpendicular to $\mathbf r$, with $\sqrt{\mu/r}<v<\sqrt{2\mu/r}$. Its path will be

options.text: An ellipse with this point at apogee
An ellipse with this point at perigee

questions.correctOptionText: An ellipse with this point at perigee

distractorRationale.a: Slower than circular speed would make this point apogee.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: faster than circular means it will move outward from this point, which is perigee.

questions.explanation: At a speed above circular but below escape, the total energy is negative (bound) but larger than the circular value, so the orbit is an ellipse. Since the velocity is perpendicular to $\mathbf r$, this point is an apsis, and the speed exceeds circular speed there, so it is perigee.

questions.stem: A satellite is in a circular orbit 800 km above Earth's surface. Taking $\mu=3.986\times10^{14}$ m$^3$/s$^2$ and $R_E=6371$ km, find its orbital speed in m/s.
questions.explanation: The orbit radius is $6371+800=7171$ km, so $v=\sqrt{3.986\times10^{14}/7.171\times10^6}=\sqrt{5.558\times10^7}=7456$ m/s. This is slightly below the low-orbit speed at 400 km because the orbit is higher.

questions.stem: Mars has gravitational parameter $\mu=4.283\times10^{13}$ m$^3$/s$^2$ (typical value) and mean radius $3.390\times10^6$ m. Find the escape speed from its surface in m/s.
questions.explanation: $v_{esc}=\sqrt{2\mu/R}=\sqrt{2(4.283\times10^{13})/3.390\times10^6}=\sqrt{2.527\times10^7}=5027$ m/s, about 5.0 km/s. This is less than half Earth's escape speed because Mars is smaller and less massive.

questions.stem: A satellite is at perigee radius $7.5\times10^6$ m moving at 9000 m/s (perpendicular to the radius), in orbit about Earth with $\mu=3.986\times10^{14}$ m$^3$/s$^2$. Find its speed at apogee in m/s.
questions.explanation: From energy, $\tfrac12v_p^2-\mu/r_p=-1.265\times10^7$ J/kg, which gives the apogee radius $r_a=r_p/(2\mu/(r_pv_p^2)-1)=7.5\times10^6/0.3123=2.402\times10^7$ m. Then $v_a=v_pr_p/r_a=9000(7.5\times10^6)/(2.402\times10^7)=2810$ m/s.

questions.stem: State the two conservation laws that govern motion in an elliptical orbit about a fixed attracting body and use them to derive the speed at perigee in terms of the perigee and apogee radii. Explain why the satellite is fastest at perigee.
markingGuide: Angular momentum conserved (central force): $r_pv_p=r_av_a$ since velocity is perpendicular to $\mathbf r$ at the apsides.
Perigee has smallest $r$, so by $v=h/r$ the speed is largest there.
Physical interpretation: potential energy is lowest at perigee so kinetic energy is highest.
questions.explanation: Two unknowns (the two apsis speeds) need two equations, supplied by angular momentum and energy. The inverse relation between $v$ and $r$ at the apsides explains why the speed is greatest at perigee.

questions.stem: Derive the circular-orbit speed and escape speed from the inverse-square gravitational force and the energy equation. State clearly the assumptions, and explain why the escape speed does not depend on the direction of launch.
markingGuide: Energy per unit mass $\varepsilon=v^2/2-\mu/r$; escape needs $\varepsilon\ge0$ so that $v\to0$ or more as $r\to\infty$.
Direction independence: energy is a scalar, so only the launch speed matters, as long as the path does not hit the planet.
Assumptions: spherical non-rotating central body, point satellite, no drag or other bodies.
questions.explanation: The first result comes from Newton's second law along the radius, the second from energy conservation. Energy is a scalar, so the direction of launch does not matter for escape.
